moTa: From the Kitchen Gods' farewell on the 23rd of the last lunar month to the first full moon of the new year, An Nhiên Temple wears its spring colors. It is a season for tidying the home and the heart, thanking the old year, keeping a quiet New Year's Eve and starting the new year gently. Here, lucky envelopes hold kind wishes, and a fresh green sprig reminds us to grow what is good.

loiChao.noiDung: Spring has reached the temple yard. Come in, shake off the road and rest awhile.
An Nhiên Temple wishes you a gentle new year, warm enough and joyful enough.
Apricot blossoms are opening; the little monk is sweeping the yard for you.
The year is ending. Let's tidy one corner of the heart together.
Hello on this spring day. Have you smiled at someone yet today?
Every kitchen is glowing. The temple sends you a little New Year warmth.
The old year is closing. Thank you for walking with us all the way here.
Happy New Year! An envelope of kind wishes is waiting for you to open.
The spring breeze is soft. Take one deep breath before you begin.
The Kitchen Gods have set off on their journey. Time to tidy up at home too.
Happy New Year! May you begin with one small, kind deed.
The first full moon of the year is near and waiting for you to watch it with us.

thongDiep.noiDung: Wiping a window also wipes a little dust from your own eyes. Look outside and the spring sky seems clearer.
Give away what you have not used in a long time to someone who needs it. An airy home makes an airy heart.
Before the new year arrives, name three people who helped you this year and send each of them a thank-you.
Tết does not need a lavish feast. A meal with the whole family at the table is the finest feast there is.
The Kitchen God goes up to tell the story of your kitchen. What warm story would you like it to tell?
The old year had clumsy moments and stumbles. You are still here, and that already deserves praise.
At the stroke of the new year, try a moment of silence. Hear your breath, and the new year knocking.
A New Year wish is precious for its sincerity, not its flourish. A simple "stay well" is warm enough.
A lucky envelope places a wish in someone's hands. What is worth keeping longest is the heart inside it.
A young sprig brought home is not for holding on to luck, but a reminder to help good things sprout.
A new year does not require a new you. Being a little kinder than yesterday is enough.
Some cannot make it home for Tết. A phone call longer than usual is also a way of being together.
Sweep the house from the inside out, and untangle knots starting from your own heart. Both need patience.
Let the sticky rice cake remind you: good things need time, a steady fire and someone to watch over them.
On the first day of the year, say something gentle to yourself before you say it to others.
When visiting for New Year, listen more than you talk. Elders often just want someone beside them.
If you owe someone an apology, try to give it before New Year's Eve. The new year will feel much lighter.
Don't compare your holiday table with anyone else's. Tết is warm when everyone at home gets to rest.
Peach blossoms bloom and fall, apricot flowers open and fade. Knowing this, cherish the spring you have.
Bamboo shoot soup, pickled onions, a cup of tea: every small dish was prepared by someone's hands.
On the first day of Tết, give a family member one sincere compliment. Praise is a New Year gift too.
For your New Year plan, write just one line. One line carried out beats ten left unfinished.
Enjoy the festivities, but don't forget to sleep. Your body deserves to welcome the new year fully too.
Tidying the ancestral altar is a chance to tell the children an old story from the family.
Fireworks blaze and fade; the smiles of loved ones remain. Look at them a little longer.
If you feel sad this Tết, that is all right. Allow yourself to slow down and be comforted.
Open the door to guests, and open your heart to what is not quite as you wished. Spring is wide; so can you be.
Plant one small habit at the start of the year: drink enough water, walk ten minutes, or read a few pages.
The one who gives a wish is glad, and so is the one who receives it. New Year joy multiplies when shared.
The first full moon of the year is here. Looking back on these two weeks, which intention have you kept?

loiNguyen.noiDung: May my whole family gather this new year, and may those far away arrive home safely.
I thank the old year for its lessons, even the hard ones.
I vow to tidy my home, and to clear my heart of old resentments.
May my grandparents and parents welcome Tết in good health, eating well and sleeping soundly.
This new year I vow to speak gently, act kindly and live a little more slowly.
May our kitchen always be warm and our family meals full of laughter.
I vow to let go of one unhelpful habit and nurture one good one this new year.
May everyone living far from home have a warm Tết, wherever they are.
May every New Year wish I give come from a sincere heart.
May the little ones in our family grow up joyful, caring for others and for themselves.
I thank those who helped me last year whom I never got the chance to thank.
I vow to learn one good thing this year and stay with it until the year's end.
At the turn of the year, may my heart be still and content with what I have.
I vow to make peace with someone I was angry with, so the new year feels lighter.
May everyone who works hard at year's end get a real day of rest.
I vow to keep my green sprig like a promise to live kindly with everyone.
May those who are alone during Tết have someone visit and ask after them.
This new year I vow to spend wisely, work honestly and share what I can.
May my siblings and I care for each other and sit down to talk things through.
I vow to look after my health, sleep enough and eat in moderation.
I send my gratitude to the ancestors who built the family I have today.
May I find the courage this year to begin what I have long been dreaming of.
I vow to give a heartfelt gift of the spirit to someone I love at the start of the year.
May everyone traveling home for Tết arrive and return safely.
I vow not to let last year's sorrows follow me too far into the new one.
May all beings have a peaceful spring, and may the trees grow green and strong.
I vow to spend more time with my parents than with my phone.
May my work this year, however busy, still leave room for joy.
I vow that each morning this new year, I will wake up, smile and say thank you first.
On this first full moon, may my heart feel whole and peaceful like the moon.

nhiemVu.moTa: On the 23rd of the last lunar month, set out a virtual farewell tray in the temple kitchen and write one warm thing about your own kitchen.
nhiemVu.phanThuong: A glowing hearth for the temple kitchen

nhiemVu.ten: Tidy the home, tidy the heart
nhiemVu.moTa: Sweep the virtual temple yard, then write down one thing you want to let go of before the new year.
nhiemVu.phanThuong: A small bamboo broom hung by the porch

nhiemVu.moTa: Write three things you are grateful for from the past year and hang them on the Wishing Tree.
nhiemVu.phanThuong: A red silk ribbon on the Wishing Tree

nhiemVu.ten: Wrap rice cakes with the little monk
nhiemVu.moTa: Help the little monk lay the leaves, measure the rice and wrap a virtual bánh chưng to share with temple visitors.
nhiemVu.phanThuong: A plate of green rice cakes on the tea table

nhiemVu.moTa: Sit quietly for 5 minutes listening to the temple bell as the old year turns into the new.
nhiemVu.phanThuong: A New Year's Eve lantern in the yard

nhiemVu.moTa: Write a New Year wish, tuck it into a virtual red envelope and send it to a friend in the app.
nhiemVu.phanThuong: A red envelope embroidered with apricot blossoms

nhiemVu.moTa: Pick a young sprig in the temple garden and give it a meaning: one good thing you want to grow.
nhiemVu.phanThuong: A vase of fresh sprigs by the window

nhiemVu.ten: New Year wishes for loved ones
nhiemVu.moTa: Call or message a sincere wish to a grandparent, parent or a friend you have not seen in a while.
nhiemVu.phanThuong: Red couplets on both sides of the gate

nhiemVu.ten: First fortune stick of the year
nhiemVu.moTa: Draw a fortune stick for the new year and note one intention you take from its advice.
nhiemVu.phanThuong: A lacquered fortune-stick cylinder on the altar

nhiemVu.ten: First full moon of the year
nhiemVu.moTa: On the 15th night of the first lunar month, step into the temple yard, watch the moon and review your New Year intentions.

trangTri: Yellow apricot blossoms before the main hall
A pot of pink peach blossoms by the triple gate
Red couplets on both sides of the gate
A five-fruit tray on the altar
A bamboo New Year pole in the yard
Green rice cakes stacked on a bamboo tray
Red envelopes hanging on the Wishing Tree
A vase of fresh sprigs by the window
A glowing hearth in the temple kitchen
Pots of yellow chrysanthemums along the steps

tho: At year's end I sweep the porch clean
And open my heart like a door to spring's green
The old steps shine on every side
A new year arrives with joy open wide
queDacBiet.loiGiai: Sweeping the porch is a familiar end-of-year task, but this reading reminds you to tidy the hidden corners of your heart as well. Whatever still weighs on you, name it, thank it for the lesson it left, then gently put it away. When the steps are clean, spring sunlight has room to come in. When the heart is clear, the joy of the new year has room to stay.
queDacBiet.loiKhuyen: Choose one small corner of your home to clean thoroughly today, and at the same time write down one thing you want to let go of before New Year's Eve.

tho: At the year's turning, incense rising slow
I thank the old year for the warm meals I know
Into the new I step with easy stride
Sowing good seeds in kind soil, side by side
queDacBiet.loiGiai: The moment of New Year's Eve is when the old and new years touch hands. This reading invites you to look back at the warm meals and the hands that held you up all year, and to say thank you. Gratitude is the best seed to carry into the new year. There is no need to rush into grand promises; just take light steps, sow gentle seeds and tend them with patience.
queDacBiet.loiKhuyen: On New Year's Eve, spend a few quiet minutes thanking one specific person, then choose one small kind act to do on the morning of the first day.

tho: In early spring I pick a tender shoot
And bring it home where hopes can take root
The truest gift is a green bud in the heart
Tend it each day and let it grow, part by part
queDacBiet.loiGiai: The New Year sprig is only a young branch; its value lies in the meaning you give it. This reading says the real gift is the green bud sprouting in your heart: a dream, a good habit, a relationship you want to nurture. Every young bud is fragile at first. It grows by being watered steadily each day, not by one big wish.
queDacBiet.loiKhuyen: Give your sprig a name this year in the form of one concrete task, and spend ten minutes on it every day during the first lunar month.
